text: this is the case;3,9 others have failed to confirm it.25 Dietary protein restriction (see Renal Failure, p.1923), which appears from a number of small studies to have a beneficial, although small, effect on disease progres- sion,26,27 has been recommended in patients with overt ne- phropathy.28 The most important approach to slowing the progression of diabetic nephropathy is aggressive antihypertensive control.10,28-30 Although most patients will require combi- nation therapy, first-line use of ACE inhibitors has been particularly recommended,28,30 as they have been suggest- ed to reduce proteinuria to a greater extent than other anti- hypertensives. However, results from the UKPDS showed no difference between the effects of an ACE inhibitor and a beta blocker in reducing microalbuminuria in type 2 dia- betics with hypertension,11 and a systematic review31 found limited evidence to support a specific renoprotective action in diabetics, independent of their effect on blood pressure. Another systematic review32 found ACE inhibi- tors to be effective for the primary prevention of develop- ing microalbuminuria. The authors noted that although data were limited this effect appeared independent of base- line blood pressure, renal function, and type of diabetes. Beneficial effects have also been reported when ACE in- hibitors are given to patients with microalbuminuria but without hypertension,33-35 and it has been recommended that such patients receive ACE inhibitors, initially in small doses, to slow the progression of renal disease.36 Some consider that small decreases in blood pressure associated with such therapy may be responsible for the benefit.11 ACE inhibition also had a modest renal protective effect in normotensive diabetics with normal urinary albumin ex- cretion,37 and such use requires further study. Angiotensin II receptor antagonists have also been shown to reduce the progression of renal disease in type 2 patients with both microalbuminuria and macroalbuminuria, and US recommendations consider them an equal first choice with ACE inhibitors;28 UK guidelines suggest they may be used in those unable to tolerate ACE inhibitors.30 Al- though a systematic review failed to find evidence that the two classes were equivalent in their effects on survival,38 their effects on progression of nephropathy appear equiva- lent.38,39 The aldose reductase inhibitors have been investigated for their effects on nephropathy, but results have been, at best, ambiguous; a study in microalbuminuric patients given tolrestat (now withdrawn worldwide) did show a decrease in urinary albumin excretion but there was also a decrease in the (initially raised) glomerular filtration rate.40 Pimage- dine, which inhibits the formation of glycosylated end products, is also under investigation. Diabetic neuropathy. Peripheral neuropathies are com- mon complications of diabetes mellitus. The intensity and extent of neurological abnormalities are proportional to the degree and duration of hyperglycaemia.
